title: Vowel harmony, KPT & T-plural
summary: A progressive set of short, focused tests for the sound and stem patterns that make Finnish endings feel predictable.
objectives: Choose back- or front-vowel endings confidently.
Recognise and produce common strong-to-weak KPT changes.
Form regular and gradating nominative T-plurals.
Use the patterns in short A1-level phrases and sentences.

lessons.title: Vowel harmony from the beginning
lessons.summary: Learn why many Finnish endings have two forms and how to choose between a and ä.
objectives: Recognise the back vowels a, o, and u.
Recognise the front vowels ä, ö, and y.
Handle words that contain only the neutral vowels e and i.

sections.title: What vowel harmony means
paragraphs: A vowel is a speech sound written with a letter such as a, e, i, o, u, y, ä, or ö. Finnish endings often come in two matching versions. One version contains a and the other contains ä.
The vowels a, o, and u form the back-vowel family. The vowels ä, ö, and y form the front-vowel family. The vowels e and i are neutral: they can live beside either family.

sections.title: How to choose an ending
paragraphs: Look through the Finnish word for a, o, or u. If one of them appears, choose the ending with a, such as -ssa or -vat.
If the word has ä, ö, or y and no back vowel, choose the ending with ä, such as -ssä or -vät. A word containing only e and i normally also chooses the ä version.

steps: talo contains a and o.
Both are back vowels.
Choose the a-ending -ssa.
kylä contains y and ä.
They are front vowels.
Choose the ä-ending -ssä. The stem stays unchanged.
tie contains only i and e.
i and e are neutral.
A neutral-only Finnish word normally chooses the front-vowel ending -ssä.

commonMistakes: Do not choose an ending from the final vowel alone; inspect the whole Finnish word.
The letters a and ä are different Finnish vowels, not decorative versions of one letter.
Loanwords can behave differently, but the regular beginner rule covers the words in this pack.

lessons.title: Saying “in” with -ssa and -ssä
lessons.summary: Build a common Finnish place form after choosing the vowel-harmony version of the ending.
objectives: Understand what -ssa/-ssä means.
Attach the ending to a stable word.
Keep your attention on the ending rather than an unrelated stem rule.

sections.title: The meaning of the ending
paragraphs: Finnish often expresses an English preposition by adding an ending to a word. The ending -ssa or -ssä usually means “in”.
The two endings have the same meaning. Vowel harmony chooses their spelling: back-vowel words use -ssa and front- or neutral-only words use -ssä.

sections.title: Build the form one step at a time
paragraphs: Start with the basic dictionary form. Decide whether the word needs the a-ending or ä-ending. Then attach the ending without a space.
Every word in this focused lesson has a stable stem. No consonant or final-vowel change is hidden inside the answer.

steps: sauna contains the back vowels a and u.
Choose -ssa.
Attach it directly: sauna + ssa = saunassa.
myymälä contains the front vowels y and ä.
Choose -ssä.
Attach it directly: myymälä + ssä = myymälässä.

commonMistakes: Do not write the ending as a separate word.
Do not translate every English “in” mechanically; this lesson covers the regular physical-place meaning.
Do not invent a stem change: every word in this lesson keeps the supplied stem.

lessons.title: KPT step 1: double consonants
lessons.summary: Learn only the three most visible KPT changes: kk → k, pp → p, and tt → t.
objectives: Understand strong and weak grade in plain English.
Recognise the three double-consonant changes.
Produce a supplied weak form without learning another KPT family.

sections.title: One letter remains
paragraphs: A double consonant has two identical consonant letters. In these weak forms, the pair becomes one letter.
Strong grade is the form with the double consonant. Weak grade is the form with one consonant.

sections.title: Keep the ending separate
paragraphs: First notice or make the consonant change. Then read the ending already shown in the complete form.
This lesson does not ask you to predict single-consonant or cluster changes.

The complete supplied form is kaupan.
The two t letters become one: tt → t.
The weak part is mato-.
The complete supplied form is maton.

lessons.title: Building noun forms with -n
lessons.summary: Form the Finnish genitive, which often expresses “of” or possession.
objectives: Understand the basic meaning of the genitive.
Add the ending -n.
Apply a known weak-grade KPT change before -n.

sections.title: Meaning and ending
paragraphs: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. The genitive is a noun form that often corresponds to English “of” or apostrophe-s.
The basic genitive ending is -n. Many simple words add it to a stem that uses the weak KPT grade.

sections.title: Construction order
paragraphs: Start with the dictionary form. Make the required KPT change to get the weak stem. Add -n to that stem.
Not every noun changes. If there is no KPT pattern, the stem may remain stable.

steps: Use the previously learned change kk → k: pankki → panki-.
Add the new target ending -n: pankin.
Use the previously learned change pp → p: kauppa → kaupa-.
Add the new target ending -n: kaupan.

commonMistakes: Do not add -n before making the stem change.
The genitive does not always mean literal ownership; it can also connect two nouns.
Keep Finnish ä and ö exactly as written.

practiceExercises.explanation: Use the known kk → k change, then add -n: pankki → panki- → pankin.
Use the known pp → p change, then add -n: kauppa → kaupa- → kaupan.
Use the known tt → t change, then add -n: matto → mato- → maton.

sections.title: From dictionary form to minä form
paragraphs: A verb expresses an action or state. The dictionary form is the form listed in a dictionary, such as nukkua, meaning “to sleep”.
The minä form says that I perform the action. It ends in -n in these exercises, and the familiar KPT consonant becomes weak before that ending.

sections.title: One direction only in this lesson
paragraphs: This lesson uses only strong-to-weak changes already shown in the KPT recognition lesson: a double consonant shortens, k can disappear, or a familiar cluster weakens.
Other verb types and strong-grade building are deliberately left for a later topic. They are not hidden in this test.

lessons.title: More than one: the T-plural
lessons.summary: Use the nominative plural ending -t for people and things that are the subject of a basic sentence.
objectives: Understand singular and plural.
Recognise the nominative subject form.
Add -t to a stable noun stem.

sections.title: Singular, plural, and nominative
paragraphs: Singular means one: yksi kissa, one cat. Plural means more than one: kissat, cats.
Nominative is the basic subject form. A subject is the person or thing that the sentence is about. The Finnish nominative plural usually ends in -t.

sections.title: The regular construction
paragraphs: For a stable word, start with the singular and attach -t directly. The -t itself does not have a vowel, so vowel harmony does not choose between two versions.
Some nouns need KPT before -t. The next lesson separates that stem change from the plural ending.

steps: The singular stem kissa- stays unchanged.
Add plural -t: kissat.
The singular stem ystävä- stays unchanged.
Add plural -t: ystävät.
Keep ä; the plural ending is only t.

commonMistakes: Do not add English -s to a Finnish word.
Do not change a final a to ä; preserve the vowels of the noun.
The T-plural is one plural form; later Finnish cases use other plural construction patterns.

sections.title: Two construction steps
paragraphs: Many nouns use the weak KPT grade before nominative plural -t. First build the weak stem; then add the plural ending.
Keeping the steps separate makes the form easier to understand: noun → weak stem → plural.

lessons.title: Saying what “they” do
lessons.summary: Add -vat or -vät to a supplied verb stem; stem building is not tested here.
objectives: Understand that he means “they”.
Recognise the supplied verb stem.

sections.title: Subject and verb agreement
paragraphs: The subject tells who performs an action. The Finnish pronoun he means “they” when speaking about people.
The verb must agree with that plural subject. In the present tense, the he form commonly ends in -vat or -vät.

sections.title: Choose the ending
paragraphs: A verb stem is the part before the personal ending. Every question supplies that stem. Your only new task is to use vowel harmony and attach -vat or -vät.
Use -vat for a back-vowel stem and -vät for a front- or neutral-vowel stem. You never have to discover an irregular stem in this lesson.

The back vowels a and u select -vat.
laula- + vat = laulavat.
The lesson supplies the stem kysy-.
The front vowel y selects -vät.
kysy- + vät = kysyvät.

commonMistakes: Do not use the minä ending -n with he.
Do not choose -vat/-vät from the English translation.
The pronoun he and the verb are separate words, but the ending joins directly to the verb stem.

lessons.title: Building short plural sentences
lessons.summary: Combine a T-plural subject with ovat and a word that tells its place or state.
objectives: Recognise the subject of a sentence.
Use ovat with a plural subject.
Read the sentence in three understandable parts.

sections.title: The three-part pattern
paragraphs: A sentence communicates a complete idea. In these beginner sentences, the first part names more than one person or thing, the second part is ovat (“are”), and the final part gives a place or state.
Finnish normally does not use a separate word for English “the”, so kissat can mean “cats” or “the cats” depending on context.

sections.title: Agreement keeps the sentence connected
paragraphs: Agreement means that related parts use matching forms. A plural subject uses ovat. A singular subject would use on, meaning “is”.
The place or state word does not become plural just because the subject is plural.
keyPoints: Kissa on kotona. = The cat is at home.
Kissat ovat kotona. = The cats are at home.

steps: kissa becomes the plural subject kissat by adding -t.
A plural subject uses ovat.
kotona is a fixed form meaning “at home”.
pallo becomes pallot.
ovat means “are” for more than one.
täällä means “here” and does not change.

commonMistakes: Do not use on (“is”) with a plural subject in this pattern.
Do not add a plural ending to the place word merely because the subject is plural.
Begin a written sentence with a capital letter and finish it with punctuation.
